newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil asks IADB for $6.4 bln in loans to year '99.
newsitem.headline: Brazil asks IADB for $6.4 bln in loans to year '99.

text.p: Brazil has applied for $6.412 billion in loans up to 1999 from the Inter-American Development Bank (IADB), officials said Tuesday.

Clearing up conflicting reports and government statements on the loans, IADB President Enrique Iglesias said $600 million would be earmarked for municipalities, once the borrowing had been approved at IADB headquarters.

Of the rest, Iglesias said $385 million would be used for administrative reform, $2.7 billion to reduce the so-called Brazil Cost, $2.4 billion for social projects and $851 million for the environment.
Brazil had asked that $2.4 billion of the loans be approved by June next year.

President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, seeking to use the IADB loans as a carrot to entice mayors across the country into supporting the extension of a special budget fund, said earlier that up to $3.0 billion would go to the cities and the states.

Planning Minister Antonio Kandir clarified the confusion at a joint news conference with Iglesias, saying that only $600 million of the loans were earmarked for local authorities. Nevertheless, Kandir expected the IADB loans to help swing mayors to the government's side.
Brazil's Chamber of Deputies was tentatively scheduled to vote later Tuesday on extending by 2-1/2 years the Fiscal Stabilization Fund (FEF).
The ballot has been repeatedly delayed because of opposition, principally from the powerful mayor's lobby.
The FEF allows the government to hold onto about $26 billion in receipts each fiscal year that would have been earmarked constitutionally for the states and the cities.
Seen as a key fiscal tool to help the government balance its books, the fund is used to cover unexpected shortfalls with whatever is left over being passed onto local governments.

Mayors from across Brazil, whose grassroots political power can make or break federal deputies, have protested against the extension of the FEF because of the money they will lose, deeming government offers of compensation insufficient.
The FEF ran out at the end of June, but the new bill will be retroactive.
As a constitutional amendment, the extension of the FEF must be approved twice by the Chamber of Deputies and then twice again by the Senate.
